paragraphs.heading: A living optical device
paragraphs.text: The human eye is a sense organ that reacts to visible light and so lets us see. It also helps keep balance. You can think of it as a living optical instrument. People have two eyes, one on each side of the face, each resting in a bony hollow of the skull called the orbit.

paragraphs.heading: The path of light
paragraphs.text: Light comes in through the cornea, passes the pupil and then goes through the lens. The cornea and the crystalline lens together offer four optical surfaces, and each one bends the light along its way. At the back, light falls on the retina, whose light-sensitive rods and cones turn it into electrical signals. The optic nerve carries those signals to the brain, which reads them as sight.

paragraphs.heading: Controlling light and focus
paragraphs.text: The iris is the colored ring around the pupil, the opening at the center that looks black. Two muscles in the iris, the dilator and the sphincter, change the pupil's size and so set how much light gets in. To focus on something near, the lens changes shape, which is called accommodation, and the ciliary muscle controls this. The lens hangs from the ciliary body on hundreds of fine clear fibers that pass the muscle's pull on to it.

paragraphs.heading: Two segments, three layers
paragraphs.text: The eye is not a perfect ball but two joined pieces, a front segment and a larger back segment. The front holds the cornea, iris and lens; the back holds the vitreous, retina, choroid and the white outer shell, the sclera. The wall has three layers: an outer coat of cornea and sclera that gives the eye its shape, a middle layer called the uvea that includes the choroid, ciliary body and iris, and the retina innermost. The sclera and the pigmented choroid keep the eye almost light tight, except along its optic axis.

paragraphs.heading: Fluids inside
paragraphs.text: The spaces inside the eye are filled. In front of the lens sits the aqueous humour, a clear watery fluid held in one chamber between cornea and iris and another between iris and lens. Behind the lens, the vitreous body fills the whole back cavity. It is a clear, sticky jelly made of water and proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Size and growth
paragraphs.text: A typical adult eye is about 24 mm from front to back and holds about 6.5 millilitres. At birth it is around 16–17 mm across, grows to 22.5–23 mm by age three, and reaches full size by age 12. Among adults there are no significant size differences between left and right eyes, between women and men, or with age.

paragraphs.heading: Muscles that move it
paragraphs.text: Each eye has seven muscles inside its orbit. Six of them move the eye: four recti muscles and two oblique muscles. The seventh, the levator palpebrae superioris, moves the upper eyelid.
